blocks.text: 文本、音频、图像和视频
Muse Spark Open 将文本、音频、图像和视频作为输入处理并送入其语言解码器。图像和视频帧共享一个 NaViT 视觉编码器，而波形音频则通过专用的音频编码器。它们的输出被投影到解码器的隐藏维度，并与文本嵌入并列放置，使语言模型能够生成基于多种模态的响应。

blocks.text: NVFP4 重新量化倒数表

在两个 GEMM 之间，SwiGLU 输出被重新量化为 NVFP4。此前，每个 16 元素组使用 __frcp_rn 计算块缩放因子的倒数。__frcp_rn 并不便宜：它是 IEEE 就近舍入，因此包含一个 MUFU 种子、一个牛顿精化链以及特殊情况处理。由于缩放因子字节只有 256 种编码，共享内存中的一张 256 项 FP32 表用查表取代了重复的转换和倒数计算。在孤立的 B300 微基准测试中，共享内存表将缩放因子到倒数的计算在分散访问下加速约 2.9 倍，在 warp 一致访问下加速 4.8 倍。

blocks.text: Muse Spark Open Architecture
Muse Spark Open combines a sparse language decoder with visual and audio encoders, bringing multimodal inputs into a shared token-generation pipeline.

blocks.text: Multimodal encoders feed a shared language decoder. The expanded MoE block shows feature-width compression and per-expert normalization before aggregation.

blocks.text: GQA and Sliding-Window Attention

For its 1M-token context window, Muse Spark Open combines grouped-query attention (GQA) with a hybrid of sliding-window and global attention. GQA shares key/value heads among groups of query heads, reducing the KV-cache footprint. Sliding-window layers attend to a bounded recent context, while periodic global layers retain access to the full sequence. This balances local attention efficiency with long-range information flow, without requiring every layer to maintain full-context attention.

blocks.text: Text, Audio, Images and Video

Muse Spark Open processes text, audio, images and video as inputs to its language decoder. Images and video frames share a NaViT visual encoder, while waveform audio passes through a dedicated audio encoder. Their outputs are projected into the decoder's hidden dimension and placed alongside text embeddings, allowing the language model to generate responses grounded in multiple modalities.

blocks.text: The MoE block surrounds its routed SwiGLU experts with learned pooler and unpooler projections. The pooler compresses each token's hidden vector from the model width to a smaller expert width; the unpooler restores the model width after expert aggregation. These projections change feature width while preserving the number of tokens. The router selects experts from the full-width representation, and the pooled expert input is normalized before expert execution.

Sequence parallelism (SP) partitions activations along the token dimension across tensor-parallel (TP) ranks, so each rank performs token-local operations on its own part of the sequence. We adapt the approach described by Korthikanti et al., Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models to Muse Spark Open prefill.

Cached results are reused when the same images appear across conversation turns, avoiding repeated computation.

blocks.text: Speculative Decoding with DFlash V2

SGLang supports speculative decoding for Muse Spark Open with DFlash V2, building on DFlash’s parallel drafting architecture. A standalone draft model uses hidden states from Muse Spark Open to populate its own KV cache, then proposes a block of future tokens in a single forward pass. It shares the target’s token embeddings and LM head, and Muse Spark Open verifies the proposed block in one forward pass, allowing multiple accepted tokens to advance together.

blocks.text: Kernel Optimizations

We reduced kernel launches and memory traffic, replaced the BF16 expert loop, distributed replicated projections across GPUs, and overlapped independent work. The figure shows the cumulative effect of these changes at TP4/EP4 with 8K input tokens, 1K output tokens, and no speculative decoding.

The figure shows the cumulative effect of these changes at TP4/EP4 with 8K input tokens, 1K output tokens, and no speculative decoding.

We combined the post-FFN norm, gated residual add, and pre-attention norm into one kernel. Q/K normalization reads the fused QKV tensor directly through row strides, avoiding layout copies, while query scaling is folded into the attention softmax scale.
Replace the BF16 expert loop in two steps.
Layers 0 and 61 use BF16 expert weights. We first batched the 64 local experts into grouped GEMMs, capping the main intermediate at 64 MiB. We then switched to FlashInfer’s
to compute only the routed expert work, with post-expert normalization bound to the finalize operation at load time.
Fuse normalization and remove routing conversions.

The CUDA boundary kernel keeps each row in registers across both RMS reductions. Pre-expert normalization is folded into NVFP4 quantization, reusing the quantizer’s row access and avoiding a separate read/write pass. Routing also emits packed IDs and weights in the format the expert kernel consumes.
Q/K normalization also applies RoPE and writes the decode KV cache, eliminating standalone kernels and repeated memory passes.
Move routing and norm/gate to CUDA.

CUDA kernels handle top-k routing and combine per-head normalization with gating, including a fast reciprocal implementation. This step also enables a shared graph stream. Verify-KV fusion benefits the speculative verification path; it is inactive in this no-speculation benchmark.
Parallelize RMS normalization within a row.
A cluster of CTAs cooperates through distributed shared memory, exposing more parallelism than a single CTA per row.
Shard the unpooler, then the pooler.

These projections originally repeated the full matrix computation on every tensor-parallel rank. Each now uses the BF16 dispatcher to compute a slice of the output, followed by an all-gather to assemble the full result. We use TGV for the pooler shards, which improves the final configuration with two-stream overlap.
The router GEMM and top-k selection can run independently of pooler and activation preparation. We place routing on a side stream and join the two branches immediately before expert execution.
We select tuned GEMM implementations for the small token counts and matrix shapes used during decode. Warp split-K kernels accelerate projections by splitting the reduction dimension across warps.
We tune PDL for small kernels by moving the launch trigger after their last input load.

blocks.text: MegaMoE Functionalities and Optimizations

DeepGEMM’s MegaMoE fuses dispatch, both expert GEMMs, activation, and combine into one persistent kernel. Cross-rank transfers use symmetric memory, allowing communication to overlap with computation without separate all-to-all launches.

blocks.text: The NVFP4 requantization reciprocal table

Between the two GEMMs, SwiGLU output is requantized to NVFP4. Previously, each 16-element group computed the block scale’s reciprocal with __frcp_rn. __frcp_rn isn't cheap: it is IEEE round-to-nearest so it has a MUFU seed plus a Newton refinement chain plus special-case handling. Because the scale byte has only 256 encodings, a 256-entry FP32 table in shared memory replaces the repeated conversion and reciprocal calculation with a lookup. In an isolated B300 microbenchmark, the shared-memory table accelerated scale-to-reciprocal computation by approximately 2.9× with scattered accesses and 4.8× with warp-uniform accesses.

blocks.text: Training Results

We trained the full Muse Spark Open language model on DAPO-Math-17K using GRPO on 64 H200 GPUs and on 32 NVIDIA B300 GPUs, with CPU-offloaded Muon or Adam with optimizer states streamed to disk. Each step samples 16 responses for each of 32 prompts, for a batch of 512 responses, with a 4,096-token response cap and xhigh reasoning effort. Rollout uses the BF16 checkpoint on both H200 and B300. Rollout routing replay (R3), which reuses the rollout's expert routing in training, substantially lowers the train–rollout log-probability difference: 0.0044–0.0071 in the runs with R3, against 0.015–0.020 in the run without it. After every weight sync, all rollout engines hold bit-identical weights.
